summary: Two people were killed when an AH-64 Apache military helicopter crashed near Salado, Texas, on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, the Bell County Sheriff confirmed. Authorities received a 911 call after 1:30 p.m.

The helicopter went down in a field off Dove Hollow Lane and Market Road 2843, sparking a grass fire that was "out of control" when deputies arrived. Cliff Coleman with the Bell County Sheriff called it "a violent crash."
Authorities evacuated several homes near the crash site and shut down Market Road 2843. An Army Fort Hood release confirmed the aircraft was an AH-64 Apache based at Fort Hood.
"Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts," Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven, acting commanding general, said. An investigation into the crash is ongoing.
Although the fire is still burning, authorities reported no buildings or structures were damaged. Investigators have not yet determined where the helicopter was headed on Wednesday.
title: Source Icon

summary: On Wednesday, President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her position at the end of August to spend more time with her young children.

Leavitt recently returned to the James Brady Press Briefing Room on July 16, 2026, after taking maternity leave following the birth of her second child, Viviana, in May; the intense demands of the role influenced her departure decision.
Trump described Leavitt as one of his "most trusted aides" in a social media post, confirming she will transition to a top outside advisor role; however, the president has not yet named a successor.

At age 27, Leavitt became the youngest White House Press Secretary in history when she started in 2025, having previously served as a national spokesperson for Trump's campaign, frequently defending his policies on television.

As an influential voice within the Republican Party, Leavitt will continue supporting the administration as it works to "defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections" in her new outside advisor capacity.
title: White House Press Secretary Leavitt to Depart Role, Trump Says

Trump Media launched the Truth API in July, pitching the service to Wall Street firms seeking faster access to content; the company said it is 'expected to provide the company with a new revenue stream.'

More than 10 high-frequency trading firms pay between $60,000 and $100,000 monthly for accelerated access, using sophisticated algorithms to act on potentially market-moving statements seconds before competitors.

Plaintiffs allege the arrangement violates the Constitution, calling it 'corrupt, and unconstitutional,' while critics question if a company tied to Trump's family should profit from his public statements.

Facing a $238 million second-quarter loss with $1.7 million in revenue, Trump Media views the service as a 'meaningful' and 'durable' source of revenue; CEO Kevin McGurn aims to expand sales to technology companies and betting markets.
title: Trump sued over Truth Social advance access sale

summary: On Wednesday, businessman Josh Kushner and former Disney executive Bob Iger agreed to purchase the Los Angeles Lakers for more than $12 billion, according to ESPN reports.
The sale follows billionaire Mark Walter's acquisition of a controlling interest in the Lakers last October for $10 billion, marking rapid ownership transition for the historic franchise.
Jerry Buss purchased the Lakers in 1979, and the Buss family controlled the franchise for 46 years before Walter's 2025 acquisition ended their long-term ownership legacy.
In a joint statement, Kushner and Iger expressed respect for Jerry and Jeanie Buss, committing to build on the foundation of the Los Angeles Lakers.
Kushner, founder of Thrive Capital, recently became a key figure in a private equity fracas involving FIFA's plans to sell minority stakes at $20 billion valuation.
title: Los Angeles Lakers sold to Bob Iger, Josh Kushner for $12 billion

summary: On Wednesday, August 12, 2026, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported annual headline inflation eased to 3.4% in July, down from 3.5% in June, as consumer prices rose 0.1% month-over-month.

Federal Open Market Committee officials, who voted 9-3 last month to maintain the 3.50%–3.75% benchmark interest rate, remain divided over whether further hikes are necessary to prevent inflation from becoming entrenched.
Core CPI, excluding volatile food and energy, rose 0.2% monthly for a 2.5% annual increase, while the shelter index added 0.1% and lettuce prices plunged 16.4% amid a cyclospora outbreak.
Market odds for a September interest rate hike fell to 38% as investors pared back expectations following the benign inflation data, according to CME Group's FedWatch.
Despite easing energy-driven volatility, inflation remains well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target, forcing policymakers to monitor upcoming labor and economic data before their September meeting.
title: U.S. Inflation Slows to 3.4% in July as Gas Prices Ease

summary: On Thursday, the Kennedy Center board voted to inscribe "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" beneath the venue's signage while approving a two-year, $250 million renovation closure.

Executive Director Matt Floca recommended the two-year closure to address severe structural decay, including corrosion as thin as tissue paper. The $250 million project covers repairs, new marble floors, and $7 million in restroom upgrades.

District Judge Christopher Cooper will review these moves after previously blocking a closure he deemed "ill-informed and seemingly preordained." Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty denounced the plan as circumventing court rulings.
The inscription serves as a workaround to federal law banning new memorials at the site. Trump's name was removed in June after a court order, though tarps still cover the facade.
Kennedy Center officials must submit the renovation plan to Judge Cooper next week. These moves align with Trump's broader capital remodeling, including work at the East Wing and East Potomac Park.
title: Kennedy Center board reapproves Trump’s plan to close for renovations

summary: On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said reports of poor conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East were "completely misrepresented" during a visit to Panama.

Senator Richard Blumenthal wrote to Hegseth and Navy Secretary Hung Cao this week citing "shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system."

Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported suicide attempts and declining morale on the 5,000-person ship, which has gone more than 200 days without a port call, exceeding typical six to nine-month deployments.

Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee requested information about vessel conditions, while White House spokesperson Olivia Wales stated President Donald Trump and Hegseth were committed to ensuring the military was "equipped with the resources necessary to counter any threat to the United States."
The George Washington aircraft carrier is heading to the Middle East to replace the Lincoln, which has supported military operations in the region since January.
title: Hegseth says reports about poor conditions aboard carrier are misrepresented

summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Thursday that the U.S. Navy will maintain its naval blockade of Iran indefinitely, rotating warships in and out of the region as needed to enforce the measure.
Following the collapse of a tentative June ceasefire, Washington reimposed the blockade to pressure Tehran back to the negotiating table after earlier attempts to restore commercial shipping failed.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to eight vessels on Tuesday, compared with a pre-war average of 130 to 140, while the U.S. military redirected more than 55 commercial vessels attempting to bypass the blockade.
Iran rejected the enforcement, insisting the waterway will remain closed until sanctions are lifted, while President Donald Trump asserted the U.S. maintains "total control" over the strait.
The International Energy Agency forecasted global oil supply will fall by 4.3 million barrels per day this year, as market concerns persist regarding the economic impact of a widening regional war.
title: US says it can keep naval blockade on Iran 'indefinitely,' vows more economic pressure

summary: Vice President Vance warned fellow Republicans on Thursday that they must deliver tangible improvements in Americans' lives or accept responsibility if a new generation embraces socialism.
Vance identified difficulties young Americans face in buying homes, starting families, and securing jobs as primary factors driving interest in socialist ideas, which he described as "dangerous."
Describing President Donald Trump's economic approach as distinct from traditional conservative messaging of the past 40 years, Vance noted that new investment is creating middle-class jobs.
Appearing on The Will Cain Show on Fox News, Vance argued that free-market slogans are ineffective, stating, "You stop socialism by making people's lives better."
Americans deserve a government that facilitates starting families, obtaining education, and purchasing homes, Vance emphasized, noting that further progress on interest rates remains a priority.
title: Vance to GOP: Don’t blame young people for being sympathetic to socialism

The U.S. imposed 25% tariffs on some Brazilian products and 12.5% tariffs related to forced labor ban enforcement allegations.
Brazil called the U.S. tariffs unjustified and arbitrary and requested further diplomatic consultations with U.S. trade authorities amid worsening relations.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pledged to invoke Brazil's Reciprocity Law for retaliatory steps, potentially affecting U.S. audiovisual companies and patent suspensions.
title: Brazil Opens Reciprocity Process Against US over Tariffs

The Congressional Black Caucus urged the Department of Justice to conduct an independent federal review to determine if a federal investigation or civil rights inquiry is warranted.
Attorney Ben Crump, Rev. Al Sharpton, and others joined the Wells family in calling for a full federal investigation and a thorough review of the facts surrounding Wells's death.
A prayer vigil is planned for Nolan Wells's 19th birthday on August 19, with additional vigils scheduled nationwide to honor his memory.
title: Congressional Black Caucus urges DOJ to review Nolan Wells case

summary: A federal trade court upheld President Donald Trump 's removal of the de minimis exemption that allowed low-value goods to be imported tax-free to the U.S..
The Court of International Trade ruled that Trump's suspension of the exemption for packages worth $800 or less entering tariff-free can continue..
Trump stated on Truth Social that foreign shippers could previously send packages worth up to $800 duty-free and with less scrutiny before the change..
A three-judge panel unanimously decided that under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the president can cancel privileges like the de minimis duty-free treatment..
title: Trump allowed to suspend de minimis exemption, U.S. court rules

summary: On Aug. 4, ICE arrested 64-year-old Charles Peter Billone in California, ending a three-decade flight from authorities in Canada.
Originally charged in 1991 with sexual assault and sexual interference involving a child, Billone allegedly failed to appear in court after release on a recognizance 35 years ago.
Hamilton Police Service investigators had been searching for him since, noting in 2014 that he may have assumed a different identity to evade capture.
Billone remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings, as officials also allege he is suspected of additional crimes including theft, assault, and drug convictions.
The Canadian Press reported on the developments as of Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026.
title: Man Wanted by Hamilton Police for More than 30 Years Arrested in California, ICE Says

summary: U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner and Gaza Board of Peace CEO Nickolay Mladenov are planning to visit Israel for talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on President Donald Trump's 15-point Gaza plan.
Netanyahu publicly rejected the 15-point document during a weekly Cabinet meeting, vowing that the IDF would not carry out any withdrawal from the Gaza Strip until Hamas is disarmed.

Beyond the Gaza plan, the agenda likely includes rising settler violence in the West Bank, where U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee recently condemned Jewish rioters in Qusra as "Israeli terrorists."

title: Jared Kushner to Visit Israel and Egypt Next Week with Board of Peace Officials to Talk Gaza

summary: On Thursday, President Donald Trump directed the Navy to replace the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System with steam catapults on future Ford-class carriers, beginning with the USS Doris Miller.
Trump has criticized electromagnetic technology since 2017, claiming the system is "not good" and "too complex," while frequently expressing a desire to return to "godd— steam" systems.

Reverting to steam catapults requires more sailors, complicating the Navy's efforts to fill 20,000 vacant posts, while early data shows steam carriers cost about $100 million more annually to operate.
General Atomics warned that modifying the USS Doris Miller, where work is nearly half finished, introduces significant cost and integration risks warranting "careful reconsideration."
The Navy must present plans to remove EMALS within two months, even as France and Chinese carriers continue utilizing electromagnetic catapults, potentially creating a capability gap for U.S. forces.
title: Trump Orders the Navy to Return to an Older System of Launching Jets Off Aircraft Carriers

summary: On Thursday, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz confirmed FBI testing found no methamphetamine in bags recovered from the van of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was fatally shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on July 7.

Following the July 7 shooting, ICE alleged Salgado Araujo "weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run over" an officer, though witnesses disputed this, stating ICE vehicles struck them from behind and the side.

Attorneys identified the substance as homemade electrolyte mix for hydration, while ACLU of Texas attorney David Donatti called publicizing the warrant part of a government attempt to create a "false narrative."

Witnesses Jos Trinidad Rojas Pliego and Daniel Tirado Pantoja remain in detention, while University of South Carolina professor Seth Stoughton noted agencies often "slow-walk" info to avoid negative perception.

Amid a mass deportation campaign by President Donald Trump, Salgado's death is one of at least 10 during immigration enforcement operations, prompting Rep. Sylvia Garcia, D-Texas, to call for an independent investigation.
title: US Attorney Confirms No Meth Was Found in Van of Texas Man Shot by Immigration Officers

summary: On Thursday, District Judge Mary Kay Holthus dismissed the case against six Nevada Republicans accused of submitting a bogus certificate to hand the state's 2020 electoral votes to Donald Trump .

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford charged the group with forgery and "offering a false instrument for filing or record" after they signed a certificate for Trump despite Biden winning the state by more than 30,000 votes.

The defendants claim submitting the certificate was "political theater" designed to publicize election concerns, while Holthus ruled prosecutors failed to prove the essential elements of forgery or deception.
This dismissal joins three other state cases courts have thrown out, though Attorney General Ford plans to appeal the decision and a parallel case in Carson City has also been dismissed.
The ruling marks a setback for efforts to prosecute fake electors in swing states who tried to keep Trump in the White House after he lost to Joe Biden in 2020.
title: Judge drops Nevada case against electors accused of forging certificate in 2020 election

summary: On Wednesday, Judge James Budreau ordered Plymouth County Sheriff Joseph McDonald to release anonymized health records of immigrant detainees, rejecting arguments that federal immigration contracts exempt state agencies from public records laws.

The American Civil Liberties Union sued after Sheriff McDonald denied a public records request in December, with McDonald's attorneys arguing federal dominion over immigration law pre-empted Massachusetts public records requirements.

Plymouth County Correctional Facility, the only Massachusetts jail housing ICE detainees, currently holds 479 men under a federal contract where the agency pays Sheriff McDonald $215 per day per occupied bed.

Sheriff McDonald confirmed he intends to comply with the order without filing an appeal, a move ACLU managing attorney Dan McFadden called important for "government transparency and the rights of immigrant detainees."

Reports indicate at least 85 instances of medical neglect in detention facilities since January, and 57 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since January, intensifying scrutiny of care standards.
title: Judge Orders Massachusetts Sheriff to Hand ICE Detainee Records to ACLU

summary: On Wednesday, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals restored several provisions of Texas' 2021 election law, Senate Bill 1, by overturning a lower court's injunction blocking the measures.
Five years ago, Texas passed Senate Bill 1, an election law overhauling mail-in and assisted voting, particularly targeting initiatives Harris County implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Judge Andrew Oldham wrote that plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the law, while asserting that mail-in ballots are "prone to fraud"—a claim critics argue contradicts evidence on election integrity.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton described the ruling as a "major victory," while Voto Latino and the Texas Alliance for Retired Americans called the law a "draconian voting law."
The court noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates dropped from 11% to 2.7% within eight months of implementation, data officials used to reject claims of widespread disenfranchisement.
title: Texas’ mail-ballot ID requirements restored by federal appeals court

Center coverage bridges these frames, calling it a “key” or “long-sought permit” while noting a state “roadblock.” All agree the federal permit advances the roughly four-mile project, but their divergent emphasis reflects broader environmental, Indigenous-rights, regulatory, and development divides.
summary: On Wednesday, Aug. 12, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers issued a permit to Enbridge Energy for constructing a tunnel beneath the Straits of Mackinac to house a new segment of the Line 5 oil pipeline, marking the final federal hurdle for the project.

President Donald Trump declared a national energy emergency on Jan. 20, 2025, accelerating the project's federal review; Enbridge officials described the approval as culminating a six-year rigorous evaluation process.

The $800 million project replaces 73-year-old twin pipelines with a 4-mile tunnel housing the Line 5 segment; proponents argue the tunnel will enhance safety by protecting the pipeline beneath the lake bed.

Despite the federal permit, the Michigan Supreme Court recently vacated key state-level approvals, and Bay Mills Indian Community President Whitney Gravelle called the decision a 'profound breach' of treaty trust responsibilities.

The Michigan Supreme Court ordered the Michigan Public Service Commission to conduct additional analysis on the project, a process expected to add years to the permitting timeline while environmental advocates pursue legal action to stop the pipeline's operation.
title: US Army Corps of Engineers approves federal permit for Line 5 tunnel in Straits of Mackinac

summary: On Thursday, vandals targeted The American Embassy in Brasilia, spraying messages against The USA government on its walls. Police detained one man in connection with the incident, though he has since been released.

President Donald Trump recently placed high tariffs on Brazilian goods while revoking the Brazilian ambassador's visa to Washington, creating significant diplomatic friction between Brazil and The USA.

The American Embassy stated it remains committed to Brazilians and the security of its staff. Brazil's government did not provide comment regarding the incident.

Diplomatic friction continues to impact The American relationship with Brazil at a sensitive time for both nations. As authorities monitor the situation in Brasilia, tensions remain elevated between the countries.
title: Wall of US Embassy in Brazil’s Capital Is Vandalized as Relations Remain Tense

summary: On Thursday, the Appellate Division, Second Department, ruled that New York City may continue its pied-à-terre tax rollout while a legal challenge proceeds. Associate Justice Philip Hom signed an order staying the lower court's pause until a hearing on Aug. 31.

Staten Island Supreme Court Judge Wayne Ozzi halted the levy on Monday after homeowners sued, alleging the city's notification of 17,000 people regarding tax eligibility created confusion about who must pay.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani 's surcharge targets one- to three-family homes valued at $5 million or more and condos valued at $1 million or more, with rates reaching 6.5%, projected to generate $500 million annually.
President Donald Trump declared the tax "must be stopped, NOW!" on Tuesday, while attorney Randy Mastro, representing plaintiffs, argued the city "botched the rollout" of the surcharge.
Homeowners have until Sept. 18 to file for an exception to the tax, as the next hearing on the rollout's legality is scheduled for Aug. 31 in Judge Ozzi's courtroom.
title: NYC Appeals Court Allows Mamdani’s Luxury Home Tax Rollout to Resume
topic_full: New York State Politics · New York

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes that five non-citizens were charged after a review of “suspected” cases, avoiding claims of widespread fraud; right-leaning coverage presents the same allegations as “illegally voting,” part of an “election fraud investigation,” and evidence challenging assurances of “clean voter lists” and “secure elections.” Its sarcastic phrase “That Thing” and “claims never happens” attacks Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, creating a confrontational tone absent from the left’s restrained framing.
Center coverage adds legal caution through “allegedly” and context: 10 cases closed, 22 under review, amid broader federal scrutiny.
All agree on five charges and the state referral, reflecting a larger divide over election integrity, immigration, and institutional trust.
summary: On Thursday, Aug. 13, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced criminal charges against five non-citizens and one U.S. citizen for illegal voting or registration activities linked to the 2024 election.
Nessel's office investigated 38 suspected cases of non-citizen voting or "adjacent conduct in elections spanning from 2009 to 2025," following referrals from Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson.

Among those charged, Robert Piva allegedly claimed his vote was an "experiment concerning voter fraud," while Kimberly DiDonato, a U.S. citizen, allegedly registered her non-citizen husband to test the system.
Nessel emphasized her office is "upholding election integrity" while noting 10 cases were closed without charges and 22 remain under active review.
These actions follow a push by Republican President Donald Trump 's administration to scrutinize voter rolls and implement new proof-of-citizenship standards for voters across the country.
title: Michigan Charges Five Noncitizens Over Alleged Illegal Voting in 2024 Election

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds two Palestinian deaths, “fatalities,” and the first deadly strike in over a week, linking the event to reduced attacks and U.S. pressure; center-leaning framing instead stresses Abu Kamil’s alleged October 7 role and presents a “targeted” operation against a “terrorist.” Right-leaning accounts oscillate between security language such as “eliminated” and condemnatory terms like “assassination,” “new crime,” and “occupation army,” while emphasizing his police-chief identity and the strike’s occurrence “despite truce.” The pivotal divide is whether Abu Kamil was chiefly a victimized police official or a Hamas commander warranting attack.

All perspectives agree an Israeli strike killed two people, but their emphasis reflects broader disputes over civilian protection, Israeli security, ceasefire obligations, and geopolitical accountability.
summary: On Thursday, Israeli airstrikes killed two Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, including a senior police official, marking the first reported fatalities in over a week as the military scaled back operations under pressure from President Donald Trump.

Last month, President Trump announced a breakthrough in his Gaza plan, involving an International Stabilization Force and a new Palestinian police force, which Israel and Hamas ostensibly accepted to end the two-year war.

Later on Thursday, an Israeli drone launched three missiles against a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing the head of the Gaza City police force, while a separate strike in Khan Younis wounded one person.

The Hamas-led interior ministry confirmed the "assassination" of police colonel Jamal Abu Kmail, while the Israeli military stated the Khan Younis strike targeted a Hamas commander planning an attack on its troops.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu recently rejected the Trump Gaza plan during televised remarks, complicating efforts to maintain the ceasefire while Israel continues targeting members of the Hamas-led police force.
title: IDF Kills Hamas Commander Who Invaded Israel on October 7 in Targeted Gaza Strike

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames a regulator’s inquiry through “alleged links,” cooperation, and the foundation’s prior serious-incident report, while right-leaning outlets use “sham organisation,” “bankrolling terror group,” and “under the guise of aid” to portray deliberate Hamas financing.
Center coverage bridges them, detailing alleged cash or humanitarian-supply transfers, concealed beneficiaries, and manipulated records or photographs.

Right reporting contrasts those claims with the foundation’s stated humanitarian, educational, religious, and welfare mission; across perspectives, evidence, defenses, and adjudication remain unclear.
All emphasize the Charity Commission inquiry and alleged Hamas connections, revealing tensions over aid, Muslim institutions, terrorism, and evidentiary caution.
summary: The Charity Commission launched a statutory inquiry yesterday into the Croydon-based Al-Khair Foundation to investigate alleged links to Hamas . Regulators are assessing whether trustees exercised adequate due diligence on partners and the use of funds.

Following the July 31 arrest of Turkish national Mohammad Yousef Hasna, Counter Terror Policing London executed two search warrants at addresses in Croydon. Prosecutors allege Hasna conspired to funnel money and supplies to Hamas through a sham humanitarian organization.

Hasna, 45, faces United States charges of conspiring to finance terrorism, with each count carrying a maximum 20-year prison sentence. The Al-Khair Foundation is subject to a legal order restricting certain financial transactions without Charity Commission consent.
The Al-Khair Foundation stated it is "co-operating fully" with the inquiry and maintains that Hasna is not an employee but works with one of its global partners to deliver aid in Gaza.

Reporting more than £74 million in income for the financial year ending July 31, 2025, the foundation's substantial revenue underscores the inquiry's significance. Regulators must determine whether trustees conducted proper due diligence on partners and charitable resource allocation.
title: UK Charity Probed Over Hamas Financing Links
Questions about Sydney protest spark tense exchange at royal commission

bias: Left- and right-leaning headlines converge on a restrained account: Apple is training a China-specific model with Alibaba’s support, shifting from third-party systems, with “sources say” preserving uncertainty.
Neither uses partisan cues such as “crisis” or “slammed,” so their divergence is limited; both de-emphasize competitiveness, regulation, and U.S.-China tensions.

Center coverage adds “EXCLUSIVE” as a report-framing device—not a claim that the collaboration is exclusive—and calls it “groundbreaking,” linking the proprietary project to market competition and geopolitical constraints.
Across perspectives, the shared emphasis is Apple’s strategic China pivot, while differences reflect narrow technical reporting versus broader commercial and geopolitical context.
summary: On August 14, Reuters reported that Apple trained a large language model specifically for the China market in partnership with Alibaba Group, departing from its reliance on third-party models.

To secure greater control over the AI experience in its most competitive overseas market, Apple developed the China-tailored model to compete against local rivals like Huawei that already offer AI-equipped handsets.
The Cyberspace Administration of China registered Apple's generative AI service last month, making Apple the first foreign firm approved to offer a proprietary AI model in the country.
In February 2025, Alibaba chairman Joe Tsai confirmed the partnership, stating, "In the end they chose to do business with us." Alibaba's shares rose about 4% in July on the news.

Apple Intelligence is expected to launch in China in the coming months following an iOS update. Last week, the company briefly published then deleted a Chinese-language guide for connecting Qwen to Siri and Writing Tools.
title: Apple trains its own AI model for China market with Alibaba's support: Report

bias: The center-leaning account frames HHS referrals as responses to “possible” legal violations, while right-leaning coverage expands them into a morality-and-crime narrative: more than 225 institutions allegedly profited through miscoding and tens of millions in insurance fraud.

Its rhetoric—“child sex changes,” “wolves in white coats,” “mutilating,” “radical gender ideologies,” and “should go to prison”—casts providers as predatory and ideological; the center’s “$50M…bombshell” is sensational but more restrained.
The pivotal divide is whether gender-affirming care is portrayed as contested treatment or abusive experimentation.

Both emphasize the HHS report, Kennedy, Vance, referrals, puberty blockers, and alleged billing violations, reflecting broader disputes over medicine, children, government power, and transgender rights.
summary: The Department of Health and Human Services released a report accusing pediatric gender-affirming care providers of committing nearly $50 million in insurance fraud between 2015 and 2025 by using misleading billing codes for treatments such as puberty blockers.

The report alleges that over 225 hospitals and clinics billed insurance companies around $120 million since 2019 for gender-related medical procedures, including surgeries and hormone therapies for minors.
Vice President JD Vance has referred the allegations to the Department of Justice, calling for a federal criminal investigation into healthcare providers accused of fraudulent billing practices.

The report and HHS officials criticize these medical practices for being driven by financial incentives and ideology rather than patient welfare, highlighting concerns about lack of proper counseling, informed consent, and potential lifelong physical and psychological harm to minors.
title: HHS Review Examines $50 Million in Puberty-Blocker Treatments

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the investigation as political retaliation and collective punishment, using “spied,” “murdering,” “outrageous,” and “Trump’s Government” while stressing protesters, unions , churches, and climate groups.

Right-Leaning coverage emphasizes court-documented methods—recorded conversations, Signal-chat infiltration, and financial-record searches—describing a “wide-ranging surveillance effort” during Operation Metro Surge without foregrounding condemnation.

Center coverage is narrower, highlighting Homeland Security’s St. Paul investigation, liberal targets, and its timing four days after Alex Pretti’s fatal shooting, while de-emphasizing investigative techniques and Metro Surge.
Left and right nevertheless converge on extensive monitoring of progressive organizations and labor groups.
summary: Defense attorneys filed documents Thursday revealing that Homeland Security Investigations secretly infiltrated churches and labor unions as part of a wide-ranging surveillance effort during Operation Metro Surge, according to The New York Times.
Undercover agents surveilled meetings, recorded Signal chats, and used administrative subpoenas to seize financial records from the Service Employees International Union and Sunrise Movement.
Defense attorney Kevin Raich wrote that federal agents charged the group as part of a broad campaign of "abuses" targeting ordinary citizens and left-leaning organizations.

Surveillance programs dubbed "Operation Puppet Master" and "Operation Whipple Shield" extend far beyond the 15 indicted Minnesotans, as attorneys seek additional investigative reports and Clearview AI data.
title: U.S. Investigated Left-Leaning Groups During Minnesota Immigration Crackdown: NYT

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the “Trump admin” and reads “Clean hands, Dirty $” as a potentially political protest, while right-leaning coverage frames the same incident as an assault on a “sacred” veterans memorial, calling perpetrators “vandals” and the act “deranged,” “disgusting,” or “desecration.” Center coverage de-emphasizes partisan interpretation, stressing “potential vandalism ,” police investigation, closure, and veterans’ condemnation.
The pivotal divide is whether the graffiti signals political criticism or irrational civic disorder, with the right linking it to Washington’s broader appearance and Trump’s restoration efforts.
All perspectives emphasize bubbles, bright graffiti, official investigation, and concern over damage to a national symbol, reflecting wider disputes over protest, patriotism, and public order.
summary: On Thursday, the World War II Memorial in Washington was vandalized with soap in its fountains and graffiti on the stonework. Reports of bubbles surfacing in the water began around 3 p.m.

The memorial sits on the National Mall, a focus of President Donald Trump's recent efforts to refurbish capital landmarks. A $4 million renovation project updated the fountains and lighting before the site reopened in mid-May.
Photos shared with FOX showed bright green and pink paint on the stonework, including a message spray-painted in red and green stating, "Clean hands, dirty money."

The Interior Department called the vandalism a "disgrace," stating, "The vandalism that occurred is an utter disgrace and will not be tolerated." Park Police have closed the area and are investigating.
Officials vowed to find the person responsible, emphasizing the memorial honors the service of members of the Armed Forces and over 400,000 Americans who gave the ultimate sacrifice in WWII.
title: World War II Memorial on the National Mall vandalized with pink spray paint; fountain overflowing with bubbles

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the attacks as “boat bombings,” “covert CIA ” action, and possible expansion of a U.S. maritime campaign, stressing secrecy, contractors, surveillance flights, and disturbing “snuff films.” Right-leaning coverage likewise spotlights a “secret CIA program” and “mysterious operation,” but leans into anti-establishment and sovereignty concerns, emphasizing “gringos,” U.S.-style patches, drones, and eight missing fishermen.
Center coverage de-emphasizes CIA attribution, foregrounding survivor testimony and unresolved identity.

The pivotal divide is whether evidence signals expanding U.S. policy or merely raises competing possibilities; all perspectives emphasize unidentified attackers, civilian victims, and uncertainty, reflecting wider disputes over intervention and government secrecy.
summary: Investigations published by The Washington Post and The New York Times revealed that a series of mysterious attacks on Ecuadorian fishing vessels near the Galápagos Islands was conducted as part of a covert CIA program authorized by President Donald Trump.

Survivors of attacks on the Fiorella, Don Maca, and Negra Francisca Duarte II describe being targeted by English-speaking assailants wearing uniforms with American flag patches who allegedly used drones to strike and detain them.

While the Pentagon denies involvement, claiming U.S. Southern Command had no role, Brian Finucane of the International Crisis Group called the situation "even more squirrelly" given the U.S. maintains an "overt maritime strike campaign."

The disappearance of the Fiorella in January with eight crew members prompted international rights groups to demand investigations, while families of victims in Colombia and Trinidad filed wrongful death lawsuits against the United States.

Government officials in Colombia and Venezuela have contradicted U.S. assertions regarding Operation Southern Spear, an anti-drug campaign the administration claims targeted smugglers, as rights groups press for accountability over these extrajudicial strikes.
title: Covert CIA program said to be behind mysterious attacks on Galápagos boats

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds CIA skepticism, using phrases like “low confidence,” “cast doubt,” “secret escape,” and “alleged Iranian plot” to question Israeli intelligence and the rationale for Trump’s flight change.

Right-Leaning coverage instead dramatizes danger, invoking “assassination threats,” “INTEL DOUBTS,” and “secret rescue,” portraying Trump as vulnerable while praising the Secret Service’s precaution despite “low credibility” assessments; it alone emphasizes Iran allegedly knowing his hotel and the NATO context.
Center coverage stays restrained, framing officials as having “questioned” threat claims.
All agree the warning was Israeli-derived, unverified, and still prompted protective action—revealing a broader divide over institutional trust, security, and geopolitical threat perception.
summary: U.S. intelligence officials were unable to independently verify multiple warnings from Israel regarding alleged Iranian assassination plots targeting President Donald Trump over the past year, according to a Reuters report.

The Israeli tips detailed specific, high-level attack scenarios, claiming Iran intended to target Trump using a sniper, recruiting someone with a knife at a public gathering, or firing a shoulder-launched missile at Air Force One.

The CIA assessed some of the Israeli threat intelligence with "low confidence," while host country intelligence in Turkey also found no evidence to corroborate the alleged missile threat during the July NATO summit in Ankara.

Despite the lack of U.S. verification, American security officials acted out of an abundance of caution, executing high-level security precautions including a covert deception operation to move Trump off Air Force One via a catering truck in Turkey.

The report underscores growing friction and intelligence discrepancies between Washington and Israel, highlighting how Israeli threat claims directly influenced U.S. presidential security protocols during heightened geopolitical tensions with Tehran.
title: US could not verify Israeli warnings of Iran plots against Trump: Reuters

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the loss of at least 45 Reapers—roughly 25% of the fleet—as Trump’s costly “ongoing war,” stressing “easy pickings,” a “bygone era,” and weapons consumed faster than industry can replace them, while highlighting cheaper drone swarms.

Right-Leaning coverage likewise emphasizes vulnerability but pivots to Iranian air defenses, taxpayer exposure exceeding $1.3 billion, and an “obsolete” platform as war “drains its arsenal.” Center coverage largely confines itself to the estimate, mission, and $30–50 million price tag.
All perspectives converge on severe depletion, revealing shared concern over military readiness amid divergent judgments about leadership, technology, and intervention.
summary: The Washington Post Thursday reported the United States military lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during the war with Iran, with estimated replacement costs reaching up to $1.3 billion.
At the start of the conflict, the United States fleet contained approximately 185 Reapers, meaning the administration has lost roughly one quarter of its total inventory.
Gen. David Tabor told the Senate that the remaining drone inventory fell to roughly 135, noting he was "concerned" about the losses sustained in combat.
Pentagon officials are considering options to buy back drones from allies to address inventory shortages, seeking to restore operational capacity amid ongoing losses.
More than $100 billion has been spent on the war, and drone losses exacerbate a broader munitions crisis; experts warn of a multi-year "window of vulnerability" until at least 2030.
title: U.S. military has lost roughly 25% of its Reaper drones as Iran war depletes arsenal: Washington Post

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds vulnerable women and systemic accountability, using charged phrases like “systematically failed” and “sexually abusing women” to portray institutional harm.

Right-Leaning coverage pivots to government illegality, stressing that prisons “violated” the Constitution while “ignoring inmate sexual abuse,” and highlighting the DOJ’s “reasonable cause to believe” standard—an important dividing line between moral condemnation and legal scrutiny.
Center coverage bridges both, emphasizing a “long-standing pattern,” “broken reporting systems,” the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments, and named facilities.

All perspectives stress recurring staff misconduct and California’s duty to protect incarcerated women, reflecting broader debates over institutional responsibility, civil rights, and governmental accountability.
summary: On Thursday, August 13, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that California women's prisons failed to protect inmates from staff sexual abuse, concluding a two-year investigation into the state's correctional system.

The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation violated the 8th and 14th Amendments, which prohibit cruel and unusual punishment, while failing to adequately implement the federal Prison Rape Elimination Act.

Examples include a guard sentenced to 224 years for rampant abuse, while an online reporting system created a "gap in confidentiality" that deterred inmates from reporting misconduct, according to Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon.

Federal officials gave California 49 days to "satisfactorily address these concerns" through expanded camera coverage and enhanced reporting channels, or face potential litigation under the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli stated, "This report should serve as a turning point," emphasizing the state must confront the persistent failure of its employees to prevent future sexual abuse at these facilities.
title: California Prisons Fail to Stop Guards From Sexually Abusing Women, Justice Department Finds
